l: SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: This document presents Self-Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation (SELF-RAG), a framework for improving the factuality and quality of large language model outputs without sacrificing versatility. It addresses a limitation of models that depend only on parametric knowledge: factual inaccuracies. Although Retrieval-Augmented Generation can supply external passages, fixed or indiscriminate retrieval may be unnecessary or harmful. SELF-RAG instead teaches one model to decide when retrieval is needed, retrieve passages on demand, evaluate their relevance, critique whether generated claims are supported, assess response utility, and select stronger output segments. The approach uses special reflection tokens. A critic model C is trained from GPT-4-generated judgments, then C and retriever R augment a training corpus used to train generator model M with a standard next-token objective. At inference time, the model can use critique scores to rank candidates, apply retrieval thresholds, and impose hard decoding constraints; this also enables customizable generation and citations. The paper contrasts this design with conventional RAG, retrieval/filtering methods, RLHF, and iterative-refinement approaches, emphasizing offline critic-augmented training, fine-grained reflection, robustness, attribution, and controllable inference. Experiments train SELF-RAG on 150k instruction-output pairs using Llama2 generator and critic models and Contriever-MS MARCO retrieval. Evaluation spans PubHealth, ARC-Challenge, PopQA, TriviaQA-unfiltered, biography generation, and ALCE-ASQA, measuring correctness, factuality, fluency, and citation quality against non-retrieval, retrieval-augmented, supervised, proprietary, and API-based baselines. The reported 7B and 13B SELF-RAG models perform strongly across open-domain question answering, reasoning, fact verification, long-form factuality, and citation accuracy, generally outperforming non-proprietary models and sometimes surpassing ChatGPT and retrieval-augmented Llama2-chat. Ablations attribute gains to retrieval, critic training, adaptive retrieval, and ISSUP-guided search, while further analysis examines customization, retrieval frequency, data scale, and reflection-token reliability. The document closes by noting that SELF-RAG can still produce claims not fully supported by citations, despite its intended role in reducing misinformation and unsafe or incorrect advice. It acknowledges contributors, support for Akari Asai, Stability AI computing, OpenAI API access, DARPA MCS, NSF IIS-2044660, and gifts from AI2.

l: large language models, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Large language models are language models that generate responses from solely encapsulated parametric knowledge, often producing factual inaccuracies despite larger models and datasets. They are evaluated across six tasks with multiple metrics, including supervised fine-tuned, instruction-tuned, proprietary, and retrieval-augmented systems. SELF-RAG enhances them through retrieval and self-reflection while retaining creativity and versatility, improving several tasks; smaller SELF-RAG models may attain greater factual precision through shorter, more grounded outputs.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is an ad hoc generation method for augmenting language-model inputs with retrieved text passages or external information. It retrieves relevant knowledge to support generation, improves knowledge-intensive tasks after fine-tuning or with off-the-shelf language models, and can decrease factual inaccuracies and errors. Common approaches retrieve a fixed number of passages, often once at the beginning, then prepend top retrieved documents to a query before models such as Llama2 or Alpaca generate an output. Its central limitation is indiscriminate retrieval: passages may be unnecessary, off-topic, or irrelevant even when factual grounding is not helpful, reducing versatility and producing unhelpful responses. Even relevant passages do not guarantee consistent generation or that outputs follow them. Adaptive retrieval approaches extend this pattern but have reduced runtime efficiency, robustness to irrelevant context, and attributions. In contrast, SELF-RAG evaluates whether sources are relevant and support the generated output.

l: SELF-RAG, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: SELF-RAG, also called Self-Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation, is a retrieval-augmented generation framework that improves language-model quality, factuality, factual accuracy, and citation accuracy through on-demand retrieval and self-reflection. It trains a single arbitrary large language model end to end to retrieve when useful, generate text, evaluate retrieved passages, critique its own generations, choose better outputs, and provide citations for each generated segment. Its central mechanism is reflection tokens: intermittent special tokens generated during training and generation. These tokens signal whether continued generation would benefit from retrieval, guide the model in assessing passage relevance, support, and utility, and enable critique of generated text. A critic model inserts reflection tokens offline into the original corpus for training. The resulting generator model learns to retrieve, generate, and critique rather than relying on retrieval for every query; it can selectively use retrieved passages and filter irrelevant ones while processing passages in parallel. At inference time, SELF-RAG first determines whether retrieval would help. After it outputs a retrieval token, it calls a retriever model on demand, evaluates retrieved passages in parallel, and continues generation with reflection-guided assessment. It supports adaptive retrieval, critique-based ranking, hard or soft controls, and customizable decoding. Segment-level beam search can use critique-type weighting and ISSUP; reported settings include beam width 2, greedy token-level decoding, vllm for faster inference, a retrieval threshold of 0.2 for most tasks, and 0 for ALCE because of citation requirements. Across diverse tasks, including open-domain question answering, reasoning, fact verification, long-form factuality, and citation accuracy, 7B and 13B SELF-RAG models outperform evaluated baselines in many results. They outperform Llama2-chat and Alpaca on all evaluated tasks, outperform retrieval-augmented ChatGPT on four tasks, and substantially exceed supervised fine-tuned models without retrieval. SELF-RAG significantly improves long-form factuality and citation accuracy relative to ChatGPT and retrieval-augmented Llama2-chat, while improving factual accuracy without hurting versatility. Its training cost is reported as lower than RLHF, and its performance benefits from training scale, adaptive retrieval, and ISSUP-guided beam search.

l: reflection tokens, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Reflection tokens are special tokens added to the model vocabulary and used by SELF-RAG. Generated alongside task outputs, they create reflections on retrieved passages and the model’s own generations. They matter because they make the language model controllable during inference: they signal whether retrieval is needed, evaluate generation quality, and critique relevance, support, and utility. They are categorized as retrieval tokens or critique tokens and include Retrieve, ISREL, ISSUP, and ISUSE. During training they are inserted into outputs; during inference the model generates them, and their probabilities can guide customizable decoding and control critique effects on generation sampling. They help tailor behavior to diverse task requirements; predicted ISREL and ISSUP were mostly aligned with human assessments.

l: retrieved passages, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Retrieved passages are text chunks supplied when SELF-RAG judges factual grounding helpful. SELF-RAG evaluates their relevance and whether they support generated segments before they affect candidate generation and ranking, while masking retrieved text from generator training loss. They can provide evidence for model-generated claims, but fixed-number, indiscriminate retrieval and incorporation can reduce versatility and produce unhelpful responses. Results show fine-grained selection and critique outperform always using the top passage, because relevance alone is insufficient.

l: retrieval, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: SELF-RAG is a process for augmenting language-model inputs with retrieved passages. During training, it can retrieve up to ten documents per input. At inference, reflection tokens can enable retrieval on demand when the model predicts external passages could improve the next output segment. It obtains passages through retriever R, processes them in parallel, filters irrelevant ones through self-reflection, then uses them to generate and rank candidate segments. Its retrieval frequency can vary by downstream application.

l: ChatGPT, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: ChatGPT is a model trained and reinforced using private data, evaluated both without retrieval and as retrieval-augmented Ret-ChatGPT. It outperforms smaller language models on ASQA, but SELF-RAG surpasses it on open-domain question answering, reasoning, fact verification, factuality, citation accuracy, and several reported tasks, while narrowing ChatGPT’s ASQA advantage.

l: retrieval-augmented Llama2-chat, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: SELF-RAG outperforms retrieval-augmented Llama2-chat on open-domain question answering, reasoning, and fact verification tasks. SELF-RAG also shows significant gains over retrieval-augmented Llama2-chat in factuality and citation accuracy for long-form generations.

l: Open-domain QA, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Open-domain question answering is evaluated with PopQA and TriviaQA-unfiltered, which require systems to answer arbitrary factual questions. The experiments assess whether gold answers are included in the generated responses rather than requiring strict exact matching.

l: factuality, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Factuality in LLM outputs matters because its absence causes real-world problems. SELF-RAG targets it through selective retrieval, passage evaluation, self-critique, and citation, significantly outperforming comparison systems on six tasks.

l: citation accuracy, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: SELF-RAG provides citations for each generated segment together with a self-assessment of whether the segment is supported by a passage. The reported results include higher citation accuracy than widely adopted RAG approaches. The work reports significant improvements in citation accuracy, while acknowledging that generated outputs may still not be fully supported by citations.

l: experiments, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Experiments evaluate SELF-RAG against diverse baselines using zero-shot settings across closed-set, short-form, and long-form generation tasks. They measure correctness, factuality, fluency, citation precision and recall, including accuracy and answer inclusion, and use 150k Open-Instruct instruction-output training pairs.

l: factual errors, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Factual errors remain a problem for state-of-the-art LLMs. Retrieval-Augmented Generation and SELF-RAG are presented as methods for reducing them.

l: large language models, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Large language models are trained end-to-end to generate task outputs and intermittent reflection tokens. In SELF-RAG, they learn to decide when retrieval is needed, evaluate passages and outputs, and produce controllable responses, aiming to improve factual accuracy without harming versatility. Their unfactual outputs can cause misinformation or dangerous advice; they were trained and evaluated with Stability AI computing.

l: retrieval tokens, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: indicate retrieval [the need for retrieval] Retrieval tokens indicate that additional passages would help the continued generation. When one is generated, a retriever model is called on demand.

l: critique tokens, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: indicate generation quality [the quality of generation] Critique tokens assess the model's generated output and help it choose among candidate segments according to factuality and overall quality.

l: retriever model R, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Retriever R retrieves top K passages from large-scale passage collections for an input when generator model M predicts retrieval is needed, using Contriever-MS MARCO by default.

l: critic model C, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Critic model C is a large language model initialized from a pre-trained model and partly supervised with GPT-4-prompted examples. Trained to generate reflection tokens, it assesses retrieval need, passage relevance, output support, and response utility. Offline, it inserts these tokens into the corpus to augment generator training data; it is unnecessary at inference.

l: generation, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: SELF-RAG evaluates and improves generation by producing candidate segments, assessing their support and quality, and selecting among them. It can also generate without retrieval when the task does not require factual information.

l: segment-level beam search, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Segment-level beam search generates multiple passage-conditioned continuations, using reflection tokens and critique to rank them by generation probabilities plus weighted relevance, support, and utility scores.

l: GPT-4, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: generates GPT-4 reflection-token predictions [from prompted supervised examples] GPT-4 is prompted to generate reflection-token judgments for supervised critic data. Its predictions are then distilled into critic model C, which achieves more than 90% agreement with GPT-4-based predictions on most categories.

l: Llama2-chat, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: SELF-RAG outperforms Llama2-chat on all of the reported tasks.

l: Alpaca, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: SELF-RAG outperforms Alpaca on all of the reported tasks. Alpaca 7B and 13B are evaluated as instruction-tuned baselines without retrieval and as models augmented with retrieved passages. The experiments use an Alpaca replication based on Llama2.

l: self-reflection, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Self-reflection is a mechanism for deciding whether retrieval is needed, filtering irrelevant retrieved passages, and judging whether model output is relevant, supported, useful, and factual. It helps users verify factual errors and supports robust, controllable generation without external models at inference.

l: controlled generation, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: is_guided_by reflection tokens [to improve generation quality and attributions] SELF-RAG introduces controlled generation guided by reflection tokens. At inference, these tokens allow generation to be guided by decisions about retrieval and evaluations of generation quality.

l: generator model M, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Generator model M is a large language model trained on outputs augmented with retrieved passages and reflection tokens. For each input and preceding generation, it predicts retrieval decisions and critique tokens; it either generates standard output segments or processes retrieved passages in parallel, with passages masked from training loss.

l: Retrieve reflection token, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: decides retrieval [whether to retrieve with R] The Retrieve reflection token indicates whether the model should retrieve passages, with values including yes, no, and continue. Its probability can also be compared with a threshold to trigger retrieval.

l: ISREL reflection token, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: assesses relevance assessment [of a retrieved passage for solving the input] The ISREL reflection token indicates whether a retrieved passage is relevant and provides useful information for solving the input.

l: ISSUP reflection token, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: ISSUP is a reflection token that assesses whether verification-worthy content in a generated segment is fully, partially, or not supported by a passage. It measures output support; increasing its inference-time weight improves citation precision but lowers MAUVE, while removing it from critique-guided beam search hurts ASQA performance.

l: ISUSE reflection token, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: assesses utility assessment [of a response to the input] The ISUSE reflection token rates how useful a response is for the input on a scale from 1 to 5. It can be predicted with or without retrieved passages.

l: generated output, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: A generated output is divided into segments and can be assessed for support by retrieved passages and overall utility. Its reflection tokens provide signals for controlling later generation.

l: output segment, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: An output segment is a generated token sequence treated as one sentence; with retrieval, multiple passage-conditioned candidates are generated and ranked.

l: critique, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: enables inference [to be controllable for diverse task requirements] Critique consists of reflection-token judgments about passage relevance, output support, and response utility. These judgments can provide soft ranking scores or impose hard decoding constraints.

l: relevance assessment, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Relevance assessment uses ISREL to determine whether a retrieved passage provides useful information for solving the input.

l: support assessment, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Support assessment uses ISSUP to determine whether the claims in a generated segment are fully, partially, or not supported by a retrieved passage.

l: utility assessment, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: Utility assessment uses ISUSE to judge how useful a generated response is for the input, independently of retrieved passages.

l: training corpus, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: contains reflection tokens [inserted into task outputs offline] The training corpus is updated with retrieved passages and reflection tokens produced by the retriever and critic. The resulting augmented corpus is used to train generator model M.

l: generator training, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: trains generator model M [on a curated corpus augmented with reflection tokens] Generator training uses a conventional next-token objective on augmented input-output examples. The loss includes original text and reflection tokens but masks retrieved text chunks.

l: inference, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
s: SELF-RAG inference retrieves more often for factual tasks, favors utility assessment for creative tasks, decides retrieval, generates with or without passages, critiques, and ranks or filters continuations.

l: adaptive retrieval with threshold, SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection

l: Lift Yourself Up: Retrieval-augmented Text Generation with Self-Memory
s: This document presents Selfmem, a retrieval-augmented text-generation framework designed to address the limitation of bounded memory. It is built on the linked ideas that better memory can improve generation and that better generation can in turn produce better memory. Rather than relying only on retrieved training examples, Selfmem lets a retrieval-augmented generator create candidate outputs, forming an unbounded self-generated memory pool. A memory selector then chooses useful outputs as memory for the next generation round, so selected candidates are reused for subsequent retrieval-augmented generation rather than merely reranked as final answers. The method is motivated by the observation that model-generated outputs may resemble inference-time data more closely than retrieved examples, while beam outputs alone add little information. The generator produces candidate pools and the selector uses model-free measures such as BLEU or ROUGE; it is trained with a KL-divergence objective. The work evaluates Selfmem with fine-tuned small models and few-shot prompted LLMs across machine translation, abstractive summarization, and dialogue generation, on seven datasets including JRC-Acquis, XSum, BigPatent, and DailyDialog. Results show improvements for fixed-parameter Transformer-based translation generators in four JRC-Acquis directions, where self-memory is closer to references and more useful than retrieval memory. For summarization, Selfmem improves XSum and BigPatent performance, reporting state-of-the-art results with BRIO and BART, including 50.3 ROUGE-1 on XSum and 62.9 ROUGE-1 on BigPatent. It also raises dialogue BLEU scores and can optimize diversity through Distinct metrics; BARTjoint with self-memory performs strongly on DailyDialog. Few-shot XGLM translation benefits from larger models and more similar demonstrations, though it remains below supervised baselines. Further analysis on JRC-Acquis En→De finds that better selector quality improves translation, and an oracle selector indicates that candidate pools improve across iterations. Token-frequency results suggest retrieval-augmented models, especially Selfmem, better handle long-tail inputs. The document concludes that Selfmem outperforms strong baselines and identifies bottlenecks for future work, while noting greater memory-selection cost on long-context datasets such as BigPatent and reliance on transformer-based generator and selector architectures. The work was supported by the listed China grants; Dongyan Zhao and Rui Yan are corresponding authors.

l: Gξ, Lift Yourself Up: Retrieval-augmented Text Generation with Self-Memory
s: Gξ is a retrieval-augmented generator that uses human-written reference as memory, together with a source, to generate a target. It may be implemented through fine-tuning for a small model or few-shot prompting for an LLM, and can use joint- or dual-encoder architectures; when trainable, it is optimized with negative log-likelihood loss. Traditional retrieval favors memory most similar to the input, but fixed-corpus quality limits it. In the reported translation experiments, Gξ’s parameters remain fixed while Selfmem improves performance by supplying better input memory, using model output to train a memory selector and for uplifting.

l: Selfmem, Lift Yourself Up: Retrieval-augmented Text Generation with Self-Memory
s: Selfmem is a novel, general iterative retrieval-augmented generation framework and a memory optimization method for retrieval-augmented text generation. It has two complementary components: a retrieval-augmented generator and a memory selector. Starting with generated candidates, the generator creates an unbounded memory pool; the selector chooses one output as self-memory for the next round. Selfmem then regenerates candidates, repeatedly improving memory and the candidate pool until validation performance converges, before producing a final hypothesis. It combines primal and dual problems, uplifts a generation model with its own output, and improves Gξ by changing input memory while keeping generator parameters fixed. It supports fine-tuned small models and few-shot LLMs, and is evaluated on neural machine translation, abstractive summarization, and dialogue generation. It improves translation across four JRC-Acquis directions, achieves state-of-the-art results there, reaches ROUGE-1 of 50.3 on XSum and 62.9 on BigPatent, and can optimize memory for BLEU or dialogue diversity. Its self-memory augmentation performs particularly well on long-tail inputs. Selfmem surpasses strong baselines and improves generation quality, but its memory-selection process requires more computational resources.

It matters because external retrieval can enhance generation quality and supports tasks including machine translation, dialogue response generation, summarization, code generation, language modeling, question answering, and semantic parsing. The described work addresses it through Selfmem, which enhances a generation model with its own output and is reported to improve generation quality over other retrieval-augmented generation models.

l: Retrieval Augmented Generation and Representative Vector Summarization for Large Unstructured Textual Data in Medical Education
s: This unit by S. S. Manathunga and Y. A. Illangasekera presents Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and Representative Vector Summarization (RVS) for large unstructured textual data in medical education. It frames clinical medicine as knowledge-intensive and argues that clinicians and medical students need efficient retrieval from large knowledgebases. l: How to Build an Adaptive AI Tutor for Any Course Using Knowledge Graph-Enhanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (KG-RAG)
s: The document presents Knowledge Graph-enhanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (KG-RAG), an Intelligent Tutoring System framework designed to make Large Language Model tutoring more accurate, coherent, and personalized. It addresses hallucination and the weakness of conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), whose semantic-similarity retrieval can return isolated snippets rather than connected explanations. Using a finance-course example involving the subprime crisis, Mortgage-Backed Securities, and Collateralized Debt Obligations, it contrasts standard RAG with KG-RAG’s retrieval of concept relationships. KG-RAG combines DeepSeek-V3, RAG, and knowledge graphs. DeepSeek-V3 is the reasoning and response-generation engine; RAG grounds answers in source material; and knowledge-guided retrieval converts student queries into semantic vectors and traverses a graph of course entities and relationships. The graph is constructed by DeepSeek-V3 from course materials and validated by a finance lecturer. Final answers synthesize the user query with both similarity-based and graph-derived context. Evaluation compares RAG and KG-RAG in response quality, learner feedback, and assessment outcomes. KG-RAG produced more complete, precise, relationship-preserving responses. Feedback from 76 university participants was strongly positive on relevance, accessibility, understanding, and comparison with human tutoring, although perceived detail was not statistically significant. In a controlled study of 76 first-year university students, the KG-RAG group scored higher than the RAG group on a 10-point multiple-choice assessment, with a reported 35% increase in assessment scores and p<0.001. The document then considers affordability, accessibility, privacy, and limitations. It presents DeepSeek-V3 as a lower-cost alternative to GPT-o1, recommends local or private-cloud deployment for sensitive data, and proposes reusing chat history to reduce costs. It acknowledges the limited participant group and calls for broader evaluations, additional academic domains and learner populations, objective quality metrics, automated graph construction, and stronger adaptive scaffolding.
